object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triage-stage event representing something broken, tracked through states from triage to closed.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an incident, format INC- plus a sequence, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence. ... Unique. And we never delete incidents

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A monitoring-system-generated or manually-raised record indicating something may be wrong.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Identifier for an alert, comes from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket that may be linked to an incident as its origin.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: Identifier for a support ticket, from the support ticketing system.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical impact/blast-radius classification of an incident, SEV1 (worst) to SEV4 (least).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Customer-urgency classification of an incident, P1 (most urgent) to P4 (least).

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can serve as incident commander.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A group that owns a service on a standing basis.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A catalogued system/service that can be affected by an incident and is owned by exactly one team.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: ServiceName
object_types.definition: The unique name of a service, enforced in the catalogue.

ambiguities.description: Kit is described as an 'Engineering Manager' who joins the call, but the identifier scheme for Person (incident commander) is not stated -- is it a name, employee ID, or username? 'Named' is mentioned but no formal identifier scheme is given.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Whether historical/changed values of Severity and Priority should be modeled (they change over time and history is kept in a separate 'timeline' concept not otherwise described) is unclear -- should the model include a Timeline/Event entity, or is only current-state tracking in scope?

source_references.excerpt: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' interim status mentioned by Owen is explicitly rejected as a formal state by Nadia ('not in the dropdown'), but it's unclear whether this represents a real business need for a sub-state that should be captured for future scope, or should be fully ignored.

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... That's not a state, that's a thing people write in the channel. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: The classification of incidents later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration is explicitly parked as an undecided business rule (pending decision by Ravi) -- no cause/classification concept exists in the model today, but this is flagged as a known gap for future modeling.

source_references.excerpt: The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.
That's a decision about what we report to the board, and Ravi owns that. ... I'll raise it with Ravi.

ambiguities.description: It is ambiguous whether the acyclic/no-chaining rule for duplicate incidents should be enforced as a hard constraint in the model, since Kit states it is the intended rule but 'not enforced' in the current system today -- should the conceptual model capture the ideal rule or the as-built (unenforced) reality?

source_references.excerpt: So duplicates should point directly at a primary, and a primary is not itself a duplicate of anything. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: The term 'owner' is explicitly flagged by stakeholders as ambiguous/overloaded in daily usage, referring to either the incident commander or the service owner (a team) -- this is called out directly in the transcript as a source of confusion, though the model resolves it into two distinct fact types.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a different sense of owner? ... it's the second collision. ... in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: 'Sev' and 'priority' are noted as commonly confused/conflated terms in casual conversation ('people say sev when they mean either'), which is a terminology risk though the underlying model concepts (Severity vs Priority) are distinct and captured separately.

source_references.excerpt: And people say "sev" when they mean either.

The cardinality of Incident-Ticket and Incident-Alert relationships beyond mandatory-disjunction is not fully specified.
